sections.html:
Binghamton is the seat of Broome County, and a sale here involves the city for permits, Broome County for tax collection and recording, and a housing market priced well below most of New York. The 2025 estimate is 46,418 residents, down 3.1% from the 2020 base. Of 21,393 households, only 44.0% own, so most households rent.

A typical owned home is worth $124,800 and typical rent is $870 a month. With values this low, a realistic price for your block depends on recent sales nearby. Look at your own street before relying on any citywide figure.

sections.h2: Floods, winter and the older house
sections.html:
Major floods hit Binghamton in 1865, 1935, 1936, 2006 and 2011. After the 1935 and 1936 events the city built flood walls along the Susquehanna and Chenango rivers, and Broome County maintains 17.5 miles of levees, many of them in the city.

  • Buyers near the rivers will ask about basement water, sump pumps and any past repairs. Gather receipts before you list.
  • Yearly snowfall averages 86.5 inches, so roof condition, gutters and heating systems get close attention in an inspection.

A house with water damage, an old furnace or a tired roof is a common reason owners here sell as is rather than paying for repairs first.

Broome County collects it. The City Treasurer no longer collects property and school taxes. The county's tax office also handles in-rem foreclosures, bankruptcies and tax certificates for the city and the Binghamton City School District. Mail goes to the county's post office box in Binghamton, and you can also pay in person.

If back taxes are the reason you are selling, the county runs an installment program for delinquent owners in danger of foreclosure. It requires 25% down and 24 monthly payments at 1% monthly interest, and all new taxes must be paid on time during the plan. A sale that pays the balance at closing ends the problem sooner.

The City Assessor handles assessments. A complaint goes on form RP-524 to the city's review board by Grievance Day. Call the Assessor's Office for the next date and file before it. A lower assessment helps whoever owns the house next, so a seller about to close gets little from filing late.

sections.h2: Permits for repairs before a sale
sections.html:
The Building Construction and Code Enforcement office requires a building permit under Section 200-9 of the city code for construction, alteration, removal, demolition and work on electrical, plumbing and HVAC systems. A permit must be on display before work begins.

  • Plumbing work in every kind of occupancy, including one- and two-family homes, must be done by a Master Plumber.
  • Demolition and work that affects a structural element need a permit, and landmark or historic-district buildings go through the Commission on Architecture and Urban Design first.
  • Street work, including a dumpster in the public right of way, needs a separate permit from the Department of Engineering.

The old grid near the rivers gives way to curving streets on the Southside hills, and the Railroad Terminal Historic District and the Abel Bennett Tract on the West Side are historic districts. If your house sits in one, expect design review before any demolition.

The city's First-Time Homebuyer Program gives deferred loans of up to $10,000 for down payment and closing costs. If title to the home is sold or transferred within 5 years, or it stops being the owner's principal residence, the whole loan comes due. After 5 years it is forgiven.

If you bought through this program, expect a payoff at closing and ask the Housing Division for the figure. The full loan is repayable from your sale proceeds when you sell inside the five years, so do the math before you agree to a price.

sections.h2: Recording a deed in Broome County
sections.html:
Recording happens at the Broome County Clerk's office in the County Office Building on Hawley Street. The clerk estimates about $190 for a standard two-page residential deed once the state forms are counted. Sellers sign the deed before a notary, and the TP-584 and RP-5217 must be signed by both seller and buyer.

Broome County Clerk fees for a residential deed
Document or chargeFee
Deed$45 plus $5 per page
Transfer tax return (TP-584)$10 filing fee plus tax owed
Real property transfer report (RP-5217)$125 for residential property
Transfer tax in Broome County$5 per $1,000 ($4 state, $1 county)

Round an uneven price up to the next $500 before applying the rate. Houses at $1 million or more add a 1% buyer-paid tax. A seller who lives out of state also completes form IT-2663 for estimated income tax. The clerk's Fraud Alert service emails you when a document is recorded under your name, which is useful once the house is sold.

sections.h2: What a Binghamton closing looks like
sections.html:
Plan the sale in this order. First, find out who you owe: Broome County for taxes, the Housing Division if a first-time buyer loan sits on the house, and your mortgage lender. Second, ask the Code Enforcement office whether any permit on the house is open. Third, sign the deed in front of a notary, and have both parties sign the TP-584 and RP-5217. Fourth, the paperwork goes to the Broome County Clerk on Hawley Street, where the recording fees in the table apply.

A seller who lives out of state adds form IT-2663 to the stack. Ask your title company which charges it collects at the table so the net figure on your statement matches your expectations. When back taxes are in an installment plan, ask the county for a payoff letter, since the plan ends when the balance is paid off at closing.

A cash buyer can work from the same list. The difference is that no lender sits between you and the closing date, so the timing comes down to the title search and how quickly the payoffs arrive.

An agent listing, a private sale and a cash purchase all work here, and the right choice turns on what shape the house is in and how soon you need to close. Listing suits a turnkey single-family home on a quiet block. A cash sale suits a house with flood history, a vacant two-family with code issues, or an inherited property that you would rather not renovate.

Before you accept any figure, pull the assessed value and recent comparable sales, price out the repairs a buyer would ask for, and confirm what, if anything, you owe in back taxes or program loans.

faqs.q: Where do Binghamton tax payments go?
faqs.a: Pay Broome County's Real Property Tax Services. The county is the collection agent for the City of Binghamton and the Binghamton City School District, so the city treasurer no longer takes tax payments.

faqs.q: How do I contest my Binghamton assessment?
faqs.a: File form RP-524 with the city's review board by Grievance Day. Call the City Assessor's Office for the date.

faqs.q: What happens to my first-time homebuyer loan if I sell?
faqs.a: The full loan becomes due. Under the city's program, selling or transferring title within 5 years, or moving out of the home, makes 100% repayable. After 5 years the deferred loan is forgiven in full.

faqs.q: How much transfer tax will I pay selling in Binghamton?
faqs.a: Expect $5 per $1,000 of the price in Broome County, rounded up to the next $500. The state takes $4 of that and the county $1. Houses at $1 million or more add a 1% buyer-paid tax.

faqs.q: Is a permit needed for repairs before I sell my Binghamton house?
faqs.a: Yes, for most structural, electrical, plumbing and HVAC work. Section 200-9 of the city code requires a building permit displayed on site before work starts. Historic-district buildings get design review first.
